Day 50 of 100 · Linux Administration

Bash Scripting Automation

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished artifact recovered

Bash turns repeated Linux commands into automation only when inputs, quoting, exit behavior and failure visibility are designed deliberately.

Architecture / mental model

arguments/environment → Bash script → validated commands → exit status/log output

How it works

The published backup example starts with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and `set -euo pipefail`, then validates required source and destination arguments before doing work.

Quoting parameter expansions prevents spaces and wildcard characters from being reinterpreted unexpectedly. Explicit usage errors and meaningful exit codes make scripts understandable to both humans and calling automation.

Strict mode is helpful but not a substitute for reasoning. You still need to understand commands whose non-zero status is expected, pipeline behavior and cleanup paths.

Hands-on reference

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
SOURCE_DIR="${1:-}"
DEST_DIR="${2:-}"
if [[ -z "$SOURCE_DIR" || -z "$DEST_DIR" ]]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 SOURCE_DIR DEST_DIR" >&2
  exit 2
fi

Verification

Run the script with valid arguments, missing arguments and a deliberately failing operation. Confirm the output and exit code communicate each state correctly.

Field note / gotcha

`set -e` has context-dependent behavior and does not turn Bash into exception-safe code. Handle expected failures explicitly instead of relying on folklore about strict mode.

Security considerations

Quote variables, validate untrusted input, avoid eval-style construction and keep secrets out of command-line arguments where they may appear in process listings.

What I learned

Reliable shell automation makes failure explicit instead of silently continuing.
